summary: Describes how Novell IPX operates over various WAN media, including the IPX WAN protocol used for exchanging router information before normal routing starts. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary:
Before two distant IPX routers can pass traffic, they introduce themselves. This RFC describes that introduction: it settles who takes the lead, which routing protocol the link will use, and what numbers the link will carry.

The same exchange works over a leased line, over X.25 and over Frame Relay, so operators do not need a different rule for each kind of link.

questions: how does ipx work over wan links
how are master and slave chosen in ipxwan
subtitle: The introduction two Novell IPX routers exchange over a WAN link before normal routing starts.

tldr.problem: Novell IPX is a connectionless datagram protocol, but WAN links are often connection-oriented and each medium establishes a link in its own way. Two routers need one common way to start using a link.
tldr.mechanism: Once the link is up, the two ends exchange Timer Request and Timer Response packets to decide which is master and which routing protocol to use and to measure the link delay. The master then sends an Information Request to set the final configuration.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives one common IPX WAN protocol covering PPP, X.25 and Frame Relay. It obsoletes RFC 1362 and RFC 1551, and it is informational rather than a standard.

today: RFC 1634 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 1362 and RFC 1551. No later RFC has obsoleted or updated it. It is a description of a protocol rather than a standard, and it was written for Novell IPX, a protocol from the era of NetWare 3.x.

sections.title: Why IPX Needs a WAN Handshake
sections.content:
The document describes how Novell IPX operates over various wide area network media. It is strongly motivated by a desire for IPX to treat all wide area links in the same manner, and Sections 3 and 4 describe the common "IPX WAN" protocol that results.

IPXWAN begins immediately after link establishment. IPX itself is a connectionless datagram protocol, but WANs are often connection-oriented, and different WANs establish links in different ways. The subsections of Section 1 describe what link establishment means for IPX on each medium, along with the other media-dependent aspects such as protocol identification, frame encapsulation and link tear-down.

Over PPP, used on point-to-point synchronous and asynchronous networks, link establishment means the IPX NCP reaches the Open state. NetWare IPX negotiates down to an empty set of NCP options and uses normal PPP frame encapsulation, and IPXWAN must not occur until the NCP reaches the Open state. Options negotiated by IPXWAN override any options negotiated by the IPXCP. Either side can stop forwarding IPX by sending an IPXCP or LCP Terminate-Request, and a router that detects this reflects the lost connectivity in its routing information database straight away rather than waiting for it to age out.

Over X.25 switched virtual circuits, link establishment means opening the virtual circuit successfully. The protocol identifier 0x800000008137 is used in the X.25 Call User Data field of the Call Request frame, indicating that the circuit is devoted to IPX. Each IPX packet is encapsulated directly in X.25 data frame sequences with no extra framing, and either side may close the circuit, which tears down the IPX link.

Over X.25 permanent virtual circuits, no call request is made, so the router assumes link establishment is complete when it is told that X.25 Layer 2 is up. If the router receives a Layer 2 error condition such as an X.25 Restart, it should reflect the lost connectivity for its permanent circuits and repeat the steps needed for a full IPX connection.

Over Frame Relay permanent virtual circuits, the router checks periodically with the switch or service provider to see whether a circuit has become active or inactive, using one of two methods depending on the provider. IPXWAN exchanges over circuits that were active before and after a router restart may begin immediately. When an active circuit becomes inactive, the router reflects the lost connectivity in its routing information database, and when a circuit moves from inactive to active, link establishment is considered complete and the IPXWAN exchange begins.
sections.plainLanguage:
IPX sends packets without keeping a connection open, but a wide area link usually works by establishing a connection first. Each kind of link says "up" in a different way.

IPXWAN is the common introduction that follows, so that the rest of IPX behaves the same everywhere.

sections.title: Primary Network Number and Router Name
sections.content:
Every IPX WAN router has a primary network number: an IPX network number that is unique across the whole internet and permanently assigned to the router. For readers familiar with NetWare 3.x servers, this is the "Internal" network number.

Every IPX WAN router must also have a router name, a symbolic name that lets routers know who they are connected to after link establishment, particularly for network management. A symbolic name tells an operator more than a set of numbers does. The name should be between 1 and 47 characters long, drawn from the letters A to Z, the digits 0 to 9, the underscore, the hyphen and the "at" sign. The string is followed by a null character and padded to 48 characters with nulls. For NetWare 3.x readers, the router name is the file server name.

For workstation connections it is useful for the client connection software to be configured with a symbolic name reflecting the client's name, so a router management utility can tell which connection belongs to which client or router. Where no name is configured, the RFC recommends a default string such as "DIAL-IN-CLIENT".
sections.plainLanguage: Each router has a number that identifies it to the rest of the network, and a name that a human can read. The name is what appears in a management tool, so an operator can see which site is on the other end of a link.

sections.title: The Initial Negotiation
sections.content:
After the data link is established, IPXWAN is activated to exchange identities and settle the operational characteristics of the link. There are two steps: negotiating the master and slave roles and choosing a routing protocol, and then exchanging the final router configuration. Once those are done, IPX routing packets and IPX data traffic start to flow.

The first exchange decides the roles, the routing protocol and the link delay used in the routing metrics. After link establishment both sides send Timer Request packets and start a timer waiting for a Timer Response. The requests are sent every 20 seconds until a response arrives or the far end is judged not to be responding, which could be after a predefined time of at least 60 seconds or a number of retries such as 16.

Each Timer Request records which routing protocols the sender supports, whether it is prepared to assign a network address to the link, whether it is a workstation that needs to name its own network and interface address on a reconnect, and whether it can support IPX header compression. Routing type options are listed in the sender's order of preference, most preferred first.

Some newer routing protocols do not need a network number on a WAN link, which is simpler because no pool of numbers has to be reserved. But an implementation that speaks those may still need to work with older implementations that do allocate numbers, so the method described below forces the older implementation to become the link master. A router that must support workstation dial-in has to be able to supply at least one network number for the workstation to sit on.

If the router is prepared to assign a network number to the link, it sends its primary network number in the Timer Request WNodeID field and omits the Extended Node ID option. If it is not prepared to do so, it sets the WNodeID field to zero and puts its primary network number in an Extended Node ID option instead.

Workstations follow similar but slightly different rules. On a first connection the workstation sets its WNodeID to zero, telling the router to be the link master and allocate a number, and it answers the router's Timer Request acknowledging only the Workstation Routing Type. A workstation never includes an Extended Node ID option. If the workstation is reconnecting after an earlier inactivity disconnect, it must be able to name its network, its interface address and its router name, so that file server connections survive the reconnect. It then sets its WNodeID to FFFFFFFFh, forcing itself to be the link master, and the router answers with only the Workstation Router Type acknowledged. Later packets in the exchange must use the correct WNodeID, and workstations always use zero.

On receiving a Timer Request, a router decides its role. The master role carries no privileges; it simply means this router asks the questions in the exchanges that follow. If both WNodeID fields are zero and both requests carry an Extended Node ID, the router with the higher numeric value is the master, and equal values are a configuration error that is reported before the data link is disconnected and manual intervention is needed. If only one request carries an Extended Node ID, the router that sent it is the master, and if neither does, the connection cannot be established. If either WNodeID field is nonzero, the router with the higher WNodeID is the master, and equal nonzero values are again a configuration error. The comparisons treat each byte as an unsigned integer with the first byte most significant.

The link slave answers the Timer Request with a Timer Response. Each option in the request is parsed, and an option that is not supported or not recognised is rejected by setting its WAccept field to "NO". The first router type in the request that the slave can support is accepted and all others are set to "NO". A router must not accept workstation connectivity to a node that is another router.

A router may support a numbered routing type while being unable to assign the network number. That type can then be selected only if the other router supports it and can assign the number, which the received WNodeID reveals. A router that cannot assign a network number must support Unnumbered RIP and offer that option.

There is one special case. If a router wants to provide WAN client access without supporting other WAN routing types, both it and the client would send a single Routing Type option naming WAN Client, and IPXWAN does not allow a WAN workstation to connect to another WAN workstation. The router must therefore not send a single Routing Type when that type is just WAN Client, and must add one or more other defined routing types, such as WAN RIP, with the accept option set to "NO", so a workstation can tell it is talking to a router. If a workstation detects that it is connecting to another workstation, it should disconnect.

A router supporting workstations must be able to supply at least one network number for them. All dial-in workstations could share one network and be given unique node numbers by the router, or each could get its own network number; this is an implementation detail, though a single shared network is preferred because it saves the router work with broadcast frames. When the router is the link master and allocates interface addresses on a single network, it should always use a unique value, incrementing for each client connection, so that a reconnecting workstation can name its old address. The six-byte interface address should have its first byte set to 2, which in IEEE address space represents a non-multicast, locally defined address, and node numbers of zero or -1 are not allowed.

If the slave cannot support any of the routing protocols in the request it received, it must disconnect the connection being established. The master, which is known once the Timer Response arrives, is responsible for defining the network number to be used as the common network number for the new link and for calculating the RIP transport time advertised to other RIP routers, using the algorithm in Section 4.3.
sections.plainLanguage:
The two ends both say hello. From the numbers they put in the message, each works out whether it should be in charge. One of them then asks the other to use a particular routing protocol and tells it what to call the link.

The election is deliberately simple, so that two implementations written years apart still agree on who leads.

sections.title: The Packet Formats
sections.content:
All IPX WAN exchanges use the standard Novell IPX packet format. The packets carry IPX packet type 04, which defines a Packet Exchange Packet, and the socket number 0x9004, a Novell reserved socket used only for IPX WAN exchanges. IPX treats a network number of zero as a local network of unknown number requiring no routing, which is useful for transferring these packets before the common network number has been exchanged. Some routers need a node number, or MAC address, for each node on a link; node numbers are formed from the four bytes of the WNode ID field followed by two bytes of zero, while a workstation is explicitly assigned its node number by the router and told about it in the Information Request.

Other vendors' IPX routing protocols can use the IPXWAN definition by obtaining router types from Novell, who then include the new types in the document. The current routing types are 00 Numbered RIP/SAP, 01 NLSP, 02 Unnumbered RIP/SAP, 03 On Demand static routing, 04 Workstation, and 05 to FF currently undefined. Option numbers only need to be assigned from Novell for the Timer Request and Timer Response packets, though the options inside those packets depend on the router type negotiated, and are defined by the vendor who defines that routing type.

The Timer Request packet always has a checksum of FFFF, a length of 576 bytes, a transport control byte of 00, a packet type of 04, zero source and destination network numbers, a destination node number of all ones for broadcast, a destination socket of 9004 and a source socket of 9004, with the source node number set to zero. It carries a WIdentifier of 57 41 53 4D, a WPacket Type of 00, the WNode ID, a sequence number starting at zero and the number of options to follow, then the options themselves. Each option has a number, an accept field where 0 means no, 1 means yes and 3 means not applicable, a length, and option-specific data.

A Timer Request should contain one or more Routing Type options, and a router should always include routing type zero if full interoperability with older implementations is required. The types must appear in the sender's order of preference. If a router receives a Timer Response with more than one router type accepted, the link must be disconnected. The Extended Node ID option should only be included when the WNodeID field is zero and the sender is a router; an older IPXWAN implementation rejects the option and becomes the link master because the WNodeID is zero. The Header Compression option is included when supported, but at most one header compression option may be accepted, and receiving a Timer Response with more than one accepted must disconnect the link. The PAD option fills the Timer Request up to the 576 byte limit, is normally the last option, and should be filled with random numbers so that compression modems or PPP data compression do not distort the link delay calculation. Implementations should not try to verify its contents. Timer Request packets are always 576 bytes, but no assumption should be made about how many options a packet holds.

Both sides send Timer Requests after link establishment, each starting its sequence number at zero, and each retry increments the sequence number. Only a Timer Response whose sequence number matches the last one sent is acted on.

The Timer Response packet has the same fixed fields, with a WPacket Type of 01 and the same sequence number as the request it answers. Unknown or unsupported options must be answered with the accept option set to "NO". If the request held more than one router type and the slave supports them all, the slave must accept the first one it supports and refuse all the others, and that accepted type is the one both ends will use. Only the router or workstation that decides it is the slave sends this packet, and workstations are always the slave. Routers must set the WNodeID to their correct value when responding, and a value of zero must not be used.

The Information Request packet is sent by the link master to the slave. It specifies the network number to use on the new link, zero for Unnumbered RIP and On Demand, the calculated transport time for the routing metric, the router name, and, for a workstation connection, the interface address the workstation will adopt. The interface address is a separate option added for workstation connectivity and is not present for router-to-router links. Routers must set the WNodeID to their correct value, and a zero value must not be used. A workstation should replace the router name with its configured name or a constant descriptor string.

For a workstation Information Request an extra option specifies the workstation's interface address, and the number of options becomes two. Routers and workstations should not refuse to use an interface address whose first byte is not 02.

The link delay is worked out by timing the interval between sending the Timer Request and receiving the Timer Response, measured in 1/18th of a second, with a minimum of one unit, then multiplied by six to bias the value so that several workstation sessions on the link do not time out, and then by 55 to convert it to milliseconds. A higher resolution timer gives better results with a similar calculation. The link delay becomes the network transport time advertised in the IPX RIP tuple for the common network number, so both ends need the same value, and it is calculated by the link master. It is expressed in milliseconds.

The common network number comes from the link master and must be unique within the connected internetwork. Each WAN call needs a separate number. If the negotiated router type was Unnumbered RIP, On Demand or NLSP, the common network number is zero.

Under some circumstances, particularly on X.25 permanent circuits, the only way to notice that the remote router has gone away is when it comes back. A side that receives a Timer Request while IPX is fully connected must recognise that something went wrong and revert to the link establishment phase, discarding the routing information learned from that connection.

When Unnumbered RIP, On Demand or Workstation options are negotiated, Information Request packets are repeated every 20 seconds until a response arrives. For Numbered RIP links the Information Request is not resent and the link is instead disconnected after a suitable delay of at least 60 seconds, which keeps interoperability with earlier versions of IPXWAN. Each retry uses an incremented sequence number.

A NAK packet says that the received IPXWAN packet was not acceptable. It is an exact copy of the received packet with the WPacket Type field set to NAK, whose value is FFh. It is used when the received packet type is invalid or unrecognised, or when a badly formed IPXWAN packet arrives. Returning it gives the sender a chance to work out what was wrong, and if it cannot, the call can be disconnected.
sections.plainLanguage:
The messages are ordinary IPX packets sent to a reserved socket number, so they look like any other traffic on the link.

Each packet carries a list of options. One says which routing protocol the sender prefers, one may carry a header compression setting, and one exists only to pad the packet to a fixed size so that the timing measurement works.

sections.title: Three Ways to Run a WAN Link
sections.content:
Unnumbered RIP is the case where two WAN routers use RIP across a link with no physical IPX network address. The premise is that nothing on the link needs to be addressed. RIP and SAP run exactly as before, except that the source and destination network numbers are set to zero. The advantage is that no pool of usable IPX network numbers has to be allocated and configured for WAN links, and that a network with many WAN links is not flooded with unnecessary extra RIP information.

Workstation connectivity has its own rules. Workstations must live on a network and have a unique interface address on it so that they can be addressed individually, but they take no part in routing and do not need to receive RIP and SAP broadcasts. That lets routers cut background traffic on a workstation link, and sending it anyway causes no problem but does slow down workstation access. RIP and SAP information should only be sent when the workstation asks for it specifically, such as for a service or route request. If several workstations share one WAN workstation network behind a router, broadcasts on that network, from a workstation or from the router, must reach all the other workstations, which involves the router duplicating the packet to every workstation connection.

On-demand, statically routed links serve two purposes. The on-demand part means a router starts communicating with a destination only when there is data to forward, and initiating communication includes making the data link call where one is needed and performing the IPXWAN exchange. A transient connection is closed after a period of inactivity. The static routing part means no routing information is sent over the link at all, no RIP, no SAP and no NLSP; instead each router is configured with the routes and services reachable through the link.

With on-demand static routing, the called router must be able to identify the calling router, so that the statically configured routes and services can be attached to that connection. The calling X.25 address can be used on a switched virtual circuit, PPP authentication on a PPP link, the router name once IPXWAN has completed, or the physical port or permanent virtual circuit identifier on a persistent data link. Whatever the called router uses is called a Remote System Identifier, or RSI. For PPP links, Novell uses PPP PAP or CHAP authentication to determine the caller.

A router running on-demand static routing must keep a database of RSIs and lists of the network numbers and services reachable through each one. Those lists determine the reachability information it advertises to other routers in its routing area, and other routers treat each such link as though it were permanently available.

The on-demand exchange differs slightly. The calling router offers only the On-demand static routing type in its Timer Request. If the called router can do it, it offers the same type along with any other types it is willing to support on the link, and the master and slave election and the choice of routing type then proceed as before. If the slave detects a mismatch in routing types it disconnects the link. For a persistent data link such as an X.25 permanent virtual circuit there may be no link establishment event at all, so the arrival of a Timer Request takes that role. As with Unnumbered RIP, no network number is assigned to the link and NLSP packets are not sent, and periodic RIP and SAP packets are not sent either, although a router must answer RIP and SAP queries that arrive on the link.
sections.plainLanguage:
The handshake can end in three different arrangements, and each saves something.

Unnumbered links avoid reserving address space for every circuit. Workstation links keep background routing traffic off the wire. On-demand links avoid both, because nothing is set up until there is something to send.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that security issues are not discussed in this memo, and it contains no security section beyond that statement. There is no discussion of how the handshake itself could be attacked, of how the master and slave election could be manipulated, or of the trust placed in the peer that answers the Timer Request.

The one authentication mechanism the document mentions appears in the on-demand static routing section, and it is about identifying the peer rather than about protecting the exchange. There, Novell uses PPP PAP or CHAP authentication to determine the calling router, and the Remote System Identifier is what allows a called router to attach the right statically configured routes and services to the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not discuss security. It says so in one sentence and leaves it there.

messages.label: TIMER REQUEST
messages.note: Both sides send one, every 20 seconds until answered.

messages.label: TIMER RESPONSE
messages.note: Accepts one routing type and refuses the rest.

messages.label: INFORMATION REQUEST
messages.note: Gives the common network number, the link delay and the router name.

items.label: NUMBERED RIP/SAP
items.desc: The link carries a network number of its own.

items.label: UNNUMBERED RIP/SAP
items.desc: The link has no network number.

items.label: ON DEMAND, STATIC ROUTING
items.desc: Routes are configured by hand; the link opens only when needed.

items.label: WORKSTATION
items.desc: A client connects, with no RIP or SAP.

data.title: Timer Request layout
data.code:
Checksum         | FF FF             | Always FFFF
Packet Length    | 02 40             | Max IPX size (576 bytes)
Trans Control    | 00                | Hops traversed
Packet Type      | 04                | Packet Exchange Packet
Dest Net #       | 00 00 00 00       | Local Network
Dest Node #      | FF FF FF FF FF FF | Broadcast
Dest Socket #    | 90 04             | Reserved WAN socket
Source Net #     | 00 00 00 00       | Local Network
Source Node #    | 00 00 00 00 00 00 | Set to zero
Source Socket #  | 90 04             | Reserved WAN socket
------------------+-------------------+------------------------
WIdentifier      | 57 41 53 4D       | Confidence identifier
WPacket Type     | 00                | Timer Request
WNode ID         | xx xx xx xx       | Primary Net # of sending router
WSequence #      | xx                | Sequence start at 0
WNum Options     | xx                | Number of options
------------------+-------------------+------------------------
WOption Number   | xx                | Option Identifier
WAccept Option   | xx                | 0=No, 1=Yes, 3=Not Applicable
WOption Data Len | xx xx             | Number of following option bytes
WOption Data     | nn                | Option specific data
